content.title: About
content.content: Cracker sandwiches are dry biscuits with a filling (cheese, ham, vegetables, sauces) placed between two layers. They are portable, ideal for a quick snack, and often used in school lunches and outdoor trips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial cracker sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Cracker sandwiches are frequently sold in individual wrappers, making storage easy.
In some countries they are called “bars” or “packaged sandwiches.”
There are countless filling variations, from classic ham and cheese to vegetarian and gluten‑free options.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Crackers contain whole grains that release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: The filling, especially when it includes meat or cheese, adds both animal and plant protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Grain components supply B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Most varieties contain little to no added sugar, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Crackers are often salty; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Fillings may contain dairy, nuts, or soy sauce—common allergens.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crackers are made from wheat; gluten‑free options are needed for celiac disease.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some packages include additives for extended shelf life, which may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cracker sandwiches are ready to eat straight from the pack; you can split them, add fresh veggies, lettuce, or a dip. They can be warmed briefly in a microwave to soften the filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a cool, dry place in the original sealed packaging. After opening, transfer to an airtight bag to prevent moisture absorption.

egg-substitute-omelet-scrambled-or-fried.title: Egg substitute, omelet, scrambled, or fried with meat and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Egg substitute is a ready‑to‑use product that mimics chicken eggs, usually made from plant proteins, starches and food‑grade additives. It can be used to prepare omelets, scrambled eggs or fried dishes, combined with meat and vegetables for a balanced, protein‑rich meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Most egg substitutes are based on soy or pea protein, which closely resemble the structure of egg white.
The product is often fortified with vitamin B12, vitamin D and iron to match the nutritional profile of real eggs.
A yellow hue is achieved with turmeric or beta‑carotene, giving the appearance of yolk.
Egg substitute is suitable for people with egg allergy and for those following a vegan diet.
When cooked properly, an omelet made from the substitute has the same fluffy texture as a traditional one.

items.title: Low cholesterol
items.content: Unlike chicken eggs, the substitute contains virtually no cholesterol, supporting heart health.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy or pea protein provides a complete amino‑acid profile, aiding muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Fortification with B12 and riboflavin helps maintain energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Helps regulate blood sugar
items.content: Its low glycemic index, especially when paired with vegetables, can stabilize glucose levels.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Free from lactose and common allergens, it is well tolerated by most people.

items.title: Soy or pea protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy or peas may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add salt for flavor, so sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Potential micronutrient gaps
items.content: Compared with real eggs, the substitute may provide less bioavailable iron and choline, requiring a varied diet.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Emulsifiers and stabilizers used in some products can cause digestive discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat a non‑stick pan with a little oil, pour in the egg substitute and stir gently to form an omelet or scramble. Add cooked meat (chicken, turkey or beef) and chopped vegetables (bell pepper, spinach, tomatoes) near the end. Season to taste, garnish with herbs, and serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the egg substitute in its original container in the refrigerator at 1 °C–4 °C. Observe the “best before” date on the package and consume within 5–7 days after opening.

fish-and-rice-with-cream-sauce.title: Fish and Rice with Cream Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Fish and rice with cream sauce is a dish that combines tender white fish, fluffy rice, and a smooth cream‑based sauce. Commonly used fish includes cod, haddock, or pollock, and the sauce is made from cream, butter, and a blend of herbs and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce often includes a splash of lemon juice to brighten the flavor of the fish.
The dish is popular in both European and Asian cuisines, where rice serves as a staple side.
Omega‑3 rich fish enhances the aromatic profile of the cream sauce.
It is traditionally served hot, but can also be baked in a casserole dish for a one‑pan meal.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish is a good source of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for metabolism and nerve function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, beneficial for thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides steady‑release energy, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including fish.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The cream sauce adds saturated fat; people monitoring cholesterol should watch portion size.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly stored fish can harbor bacteria or parasites; always observe proper refrigeration and cooking times.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cream and prepared sauces often contain salt; those with hypertension should limit added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing fish, rice, and sauce on a plate. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) or lemon wedges for extra brightness. It pairs well with steamed vegetables or a green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of cream or broth to prevent the sauce from drying out. For longer storage, freeze fish and rice separately; the cream sauce does not freeze well.

content.title: About
content.content: Similac Sensitive Ready‑to‑Feed is a ready‑to‑use infant formula designed for babies with sensitive digestion. The formula features partially hydrolyzed protein, prebiotics, and an optimal blend of vitamins and minerals to support growth and development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Available in sterile 250 ml containers that require no preparation.
Uses partially hydrolyzed casein to reduce the risk of food‑allergy reactions in sensitive infants.
Contains prebiotic fructooligosaccharides (FOS) that promote healthy gut flora.
Enriched with DHA and ARA, essential fatty acids for brain and eye development.
Clinically tested to confirm safety and efficacy for infants.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Partially hydrolyzed protein is easier to digest, lessening gastrointestinal stress.

items.title: Promotes gut microbiome
items.content: Prebiotics foster growth of beneficial bacteria, enhancing immunity and digestion.

items.title: Balanced vitamins and minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc, calcium, and B‑vitamins essential for growth.

items.title: Brain and eye development
items.content: DHA and ARA support neural and visual development.

items.title: Reduced allergy risk
items.content: Hydrolyzed protein lowers the likelihood of allergic reactions in sensitive babies.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Despite hydrolysis, some infants may still react to milk proteins.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: Contains lactose; infants with lactose intolerance need a specialized formula.

items.title: Shelf‑life after opening
items.content: Once opened, store in the refrigerator and use within 48 hours.

items.title: Heating method
items.content: Do not microwave the ready‑to‑feed product to avoid overheating and nutrient loss.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: The formula is ready to feed directly from the container. Offer the appropriate amount based on the infant’s age and pediatrician’s guidance. If warming is desired, gently heat to body temperature and test on the wrist before feeding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened containers in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 48 hours. Discard if the product develops an off‑smell, color change, or unusual taste.

content.title: About
content.content: A taco is a Mexican dish consisting of a soft flour tortilla filled with chicken, cheese, and often additional ingredients such as vegetables, sauces, and spices. The tortilla provides a tender base, while the chicken and cheese deliver protein and a rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flour tortillas originated in northern Mexico in the 19th century as an alternative to corn tortillas.
Tacos became popular in the United States after World War II when American soldiers brought them back from Mexico.
While soft tortillas are traditional, some regions serve them toasted for a crisp texture.
Chicken in tacos is often marinated in lime juice and spices to enhance its aroma.
The cheese used is usually a melting variety such as cheddar or Mexican queso fresco, adding a creamy texture.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, which supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and wheat flour tortillas contain B6 and B12 vitamins that aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Moderate carbohydrate content
items.content: Compared with many fast‑food options, a flour‑tortilla taco offers a balanced amount of carbs suitable for a varied diet.

items.title: Potential probiotic boost (with fermented sauces)
items.content: If the taco includes fermented sauces like salsa, it can contribute beneficial bacteria to the gut.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and ready‑made sauces often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten in the tortilla
items.content: Flour tortillas contain gluten, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of tortilla, cheese, and sauce makes tacos relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the tortilla briefly, then fill it with chicken, shredded cheese, and any desired toppings—fresh veggies, salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. The tortilla can be folded in half or rolled into a wrap.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared tacos should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Tortillas can be frozen in a bag for up to 2 months; thaw and warm them before serving.
